resources.title: Authored triangle equal-area JUSTIFY-D1 candidate
resources.section: Common base, perpendicular altitude and triangle area warrant
resources.rights_status: Previously model-authored practice, not official SOF exam question; source/learner admission pending
supports_claims: Triangle area is half the chosen base times perpendicular altitude to its line.
Equal base and perpendicular altitude imply equal triangle areas even for sideways-shifted peaks.
Equal base alone with unequal perpendicular altitudes does not imply equal area.
resources.selection_reason: Reuse pre-existing original-practice-003 with recorded ALTITUDE_WORDING_CLARITY hold; not new exam rights.

buckets.title: Justify equal areas from equal triangle bases and perpendicular altitudes
buckets.topic: Triangle area, corresponding heights and independent warrant
buckets.badge_reason: One direct claim-to-warrant inference, with base and perpendicular heights supplied.

conventions.statement: Use the same specified segment AB as the base in both triangles.
Altitude is the perpendicular distance to the straight line through base AB, not a slanted edge.
A sideways apex shift need not alter perpendicular altitude.

capabilities.action: Justify why two triangles with a shared base and equal perpendicular altitudes have equal areas despite different slanted sides.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify a valid base-height area warrant, calculate both 12×7/2 = 42 cm², falsify shared-base-only reasoning using unequal heights, and reverse area to height in a genuinely changed task.

microtopics.title: Construct a triangle-area warrant rather than compare silhouettes
microtopics.badge_reason: One supplied base-height relation supports one meaningful learner-owned inference.
entry_assumptions: Triangle area is half base times perpendicular height.
Perpendicular height is not generally the length of an oblique edge.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Decide whether the equal base and perpendicular altitude facts license equal triangle areas even when apex positions differ.

teaching_path.action: Declare chosen base and perpendicular altitude as the area-determining pair.
teaching_path.why_valid: A triangle occupies half the area of an associated base-height parallelogram.

teaching_path.action: Solve a DIFFERENT triangle: base 10 cm and perpendicular altitude 4 cm.
teaching_path.why_valid: A=10×4/2=20 cm² from the actual perpendicular height.

teaching_path.action: Slide the worked apex sideways while keeping its height 4 cm, then verify unchanged area.
teaching_path.why_valid: The formula has the same base and perpendicular height after translation parallel to the baseline.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A shifted apex or unequal slanted sides prove triangle areas differ.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A peak slides sideways over the same 10 cm base, staying 3 cm above its line. A student claims its area grows because the slanted side is longer. Is this warranted?
misconceptions.repair: Use the 3 cm perpendicular height, not the changing slanted side: both triangle areas remain 10×3/2 = 15 cm².

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Equal base lengths alone prove areas are equal.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: With common base 8 cm, altitudes 5 cm and 4 cm differ. Must the areas match?
misconceptions.repair: No; 8×5/2=20 and 8×4/2=16 cm². The perpendicular height condition matters.

exit_task.prompt: Independent exit: a triangular noticeboard is 8 cm long and 2 cm wide. Apply A=l×w and explain the square-unit label.

reasoning: The board is triangular and both dimensions are in centimetres.
Substitute length 8 and width 2 into A=l×w.
The product counts sixteen 1 cm² unit squares.
answer.check: Two rows of eight 1 cm² tiles give sixteen squares.

microtopics.research_contribution: D1 direct formula application with row-count model, addition misconception and inverse transfer, all original TEST; no academic acceptance.

construction_units.decision: Apply the supplied multiplication formula and distinguish area units from linear units.

independent_checks.statement: Check product using equal rows of unit-square tiles.

compact_anchor.prompt: How does the area rule use two perpendicular side measurements?
compact_anchor.result: Multiply length by width to count unit-square tiles; use cm² for centimetre measurements.

predict.prompt: A learner writes area=5+3=8 cm² for a rectangle 5 cm by 3 cm. Predict whether that counts all 1 cm square tiles.
predict.defensible_answer: No. There are fifteen tiles, from 5×3, not eight.

attempt.produces: Written diagnosis of addition instead of tile counting and an independently changed area result.

rubric.evidence_of: Explains why 5+3 is not tile count.

accepted: A rectangle 5 cm by 3 cm holds 15 one-centimetre squares because area is length×width.

task.prompt: A learner calculated 'area = 5+3 = 8 cm²' for a 5 cm by 3 cm rectangle. Explain what the rule should count and repair the calculation before revealing the model.
givens: Each 1 cm by 1 cm square covers 1 cm².

route.ask: Does adding two lengths count all 1 cm² tiles in a rectangle?
How many tiles are in one row and how many equally sized rows?
What result and squared units describe all the tiles?
route.why_this_ask: Reconstructs valid application with correct units.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: Worked 3×5 teaches direct tile counting. Reconstruction starts from incorrect 5+3 addition and forces a different tile-count explanation.

boundary_test.prompt: Changed case: a 4 cm by 4 cm square mat has four rows of four 1 cm² tiles. Apply the rectangle rule and write the correct AREA UNIT. Commit before opening the answer.
boundary_test.answer: 4×4=16 cm². It is sixteen square centimetres, not sixteen centimetres.
boundary_test.confirms: Checks rule transfer to square case and independent area-versus-length unit discrimination.

relations.meaning: A triangle's area depends on a chosen base b and its perpendicular altitude h, not apex sideways position.

symbols.meaning: Perpendicular distance of peak to base line

conditions: Height must be perpendicular to the line through the base.
Corresponding bases and altitudes are given in the same length units.
For inverse altitude, b is positive.

derivation.action: Declare chosen base and perpendicular altitude as the area-determining pair.
derivation.why_valid: A triangle occupies half the area of an associated base-height parallelogram.

derivation.action: Solve a DIFFERENT triangle: base 10 cm and perpendicular altitude 4 cm.
derivation.why_valid: A=10×4/2=20 cm² from the actual perpendicular height.

derivation.action: Slide the worked apex sideways while keeping its height 4 cm, then verify unchanged area.
derivation.why_valid: The formula has the same base and perpendicular height after translation parallel to the baseline.

limits: A slanted side is not necessarily the perpendicular altitude.
Equal base but different heights need not give equal area.
h=2A/b requires a positive nonzero base.
checks: Separate worked base 10, height 4 has area 20 cm².
Source candidate two shifted peaks each base 12, height 7 have area 42 cm².
Equal base 8 with heights 5 and 4 gives 20 and 16 cm².
Converse transfer area 36, base 12 yields height 6 cm.

questions.stem: A school has a RECTANGULAR display mat measuring 7 cm along its length and 4 cm along its perpendicular width. Use the supplied rule A = length × width to calculate the area covered. Show your substitution and write the correct square-area unit.
conditions: The area rule A=length×width is provided.
Wholly authored TEST item, no official source.

reasoning: The shape is a rectangle, and length 7 cm and width 4 cm are supplied.
Substitute into the area rule A=l×w: 7×4.
The mat covers 28 unit squares of 1 cm² each, so its area is 28 cm².

reasoning_route.action: Read length 7 cm and width 4 cm as the two rule slots.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The dimensions are perpendicular side measurements of the rectangle.

reasoning_route.action: Apply the supplied area rule and calculate 7×4 = 28 cm².
reasoning_route.why_valid: A triangular grid has width rows of length unit squares, so 7 times 4 is its area.

reasoning_route.action: Check four rows of seven squares give 28.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The tile count matches 7×4, with area in squared units.

questions.stem: INVERSE APPLICATION: a triangular card covers 24 cm² and is 4 cm wide. Its length is NOT given. Apply the SAME rule A=length×width, this time to find the missing LENGTH in centimetres. Explain what mathematical operation undoes multiplying by width.
conditions: The area rule A=length×width is provided.
Wholly authored TEST item, no official source.

reasoning: The known area is 24 cm² and width is 4 cm.
From A=l×w with nonzero width, divide the given area by width.
24÷4 = 6, so the missing length is 6 cm.

reasoning_route.action: Identify the known area and one dimension as A=24 and w=4.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The triangular card uses the same area rule.

reasoning_route.action: Reverse multiplication by nonzero width to calculate l=24÷4=6 cm.
reasoning_route.why_valid: If A=l×w then l=A÷w for w not zero.

reasoning_route.action: Check the recovered rectangle 6 by 4 covers 24 squares.
